newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank fights last stand to defend stable Euro.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank fights last stand to defend stable Euro.

text.p: The Bundesbank, Europe's staunchest champion of monetary stability, entered a damaging conflict with the German government on Wednesday, bent on sustaining its credibility as the front line against efforts to weaken the euro.
The bank issued a sharply-worded statement condemning Bonn's plan to revalue the Bundesbank's reserves and accusing it of risking a public loss of faith in the single currency.
The statement exposed a deep rift between the government and the Bundesbank which had in the past formed a common German front against any softening of the entry criteria.
That alliance had been viewed as crucial to overcoming the German public's reluctance to give up the mark.
But Germany's reputation as European paragon of monetary stability has crumbled amid mounting evidence that it will have great difficulty qualifying for the launch.

Bonn's plan to revalue the Bundesbank reserves has put it in the embarrassing position of being accused of the same sort of budget tricks it has steadily criticised in other contenders for monetary union.
Tersely reminding Bonn of its commitment to a stable euro, the Bundesbank said:

"The Federal Government and the Bundesbank have always stressed that the convergence criteria of the Maastricht Treaty must be fulfilled credibly and on a lasting basis in order to put European monetary union on a solid basis."
Bonn's move to fufil the criteria by drawing on the bank gold and currency reserves in 1997 "would in the Bundesbank's view not live up to these requirements," it added.

The bank also warned Bonn that if it made use of its right to enforce the changes in the face of the bank's opposition it would be damaging a key pillar of monetary stability -- central bank independence.

"If it is legally enforced this would mean an intervention in the Bundesbank's monetary policy. Such a measure would contradict German tradition and contradict the Maastricht Treaty's view on the independence of the central banks."

The statement was released after a meeting of the central bank's policymaking council which discussed a controversial plan by Finance Minister Theo Waigel to increase the value of the bank's reserves and use the gain to reduce the public debt.
Under Waigel's proposal part of the gain would be paid out in 1997, the key year for deciding which countries can join monetary union, scheduled to go ahead on January 1, 1999.
The plan is aimed at helping to plug gaping holes torn in the government finances by a shortfall in tax revenues amid persistently high unemployment.
Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing said the plan was "even more creative than steps taken in other countries."
Bonn's ruling coalition responded on Wednesday that it was going to stick with its plans to revalue the reserves and denied that this would harm the independence of the Bundesbank.
Analysts said that while the government had the power to push through the plan it would now be difficult in the face of the Bundesbank's opposition.

"Legally, the government has the law on its side. From a political point of view, it is going to be very difficult to introduce the plan...against the will of the Bundesbank, against the will of the experts and definitely against public opinion," said Armin Kayser, an economist at Swiss Bank Corp in Frankfurt.
